title: RAG Security Controls and Defense Implementation
prerequisites: RAG Attack Techniques: Information Leakage and Poisoning
learning_objectives: Implement document-level access control at the retrieval layer
Design ingestion pipelines with content integrity scanning
Build output monitoring to detect RAG-based exfiltration
Apply source citation and provenance tracking
Architect a secure end-to-end RAG system

post_assessment.question: Where should access control filters be applied in a RAG pipeline?
options: At the vector database query level, filtering by user permissions before documents reach the LLM
After the LLM generates a response
post_assessment.explanation: Access control must be applied at retrieval time — filtering which documents are fetched from the vector database based on user permissions. Post-retrieval filtering is insufficient because the LLM may have already processed restricted content.

post_assessment.question: What is source provenance in RAG security?
options: The IP address of the document uploader
Tracking which documents contributed to each response, enabling audit and accountability
The file format of ingested documents
The geographic location of the vector database
post_assessment.explanation: Source provenance tracks which documents were retrieved and included in each LLM response, enabling auditing, detecting poisoning, and providing response attribution.

post_assessment.question: What should an ingestion pipeline scan for before adding a document to the knowledge base?
options: Instruction-like patterns, PII, malicious links, and content policy violations
post_assessment.explanation: Ingestion scanning should check for embedded instructions (prompt injection), PII that shouldn't be indexed, malicious URLs, and content policy violations before documents enter the knowledge base.

post_assessment.question: How does output monitoring help detect RAG poisoning?
options: It detects anomalous response patterns — unusual content, unexpected source citations, or systematic information disclosure
post_assessment.explanation: Output monitoring can catch signs of poisoning: responses citing unexpected sources, unusual content patterns, systematic disclosure of restricted categories, or instruction-following behavior from retrieved content.

jim_kwik_principles.forget: Forget bolt-on security — RAG security controls must be designed into the architecture from the start
jim_kwik_principles.active: Implement retrieval-time access control in a sample RAG application and verify it works with test queries
jim_kwik_principles.state: Think like a security architect designing for zero trust — every component is untrusted until proven otherwise
jim_kwik_principles.teach: Explain RAG access control as 'the librarian checks your library card before handing you the book, not after'
jim_kwik_principles.enter: Before implementing controls, prioritize by attack risk: access control first, then ingestion scanning, then monitoring
jim_kwik_principles.review: After implementing each control, run the relevant attack technique from lesson 32 to verify it's blocked
jim_kwik_principles.notes: Create a RAG security design checklist: ingestion → storage → retrieval → context → output — check each layer
jim_kwik_principles.why: Secure RAG design is a competitive differentiator — enterprises choosing AI platforms will prioritize security
jim_kwik_principles.emotion: The confidence of deploying a RAG system knowing each attack vector has a specific countermeasure
jim_kwik_principles.speed: Use existing security frameworks (LlamaIndex security modules, LangChain callbacks) instead of building from scratch

content_blocks.title: Defense Is Architecture, Not Afterthought
content_blocks.content: The best RAG security doesn't come from patching — it comes from design. A system built with access control at the retrieval layer, ingestion scanning, provenance tracking, and output monitoring is fundamentally harder to attack than one with security bolted on afterward. This lesson translates the attack techniques you learned into specific, implementable controls.

content_blocks.title: RAG Security Controls by Layer
content_blocks.content: Each RAG layer requires specific security controls.

subsections.title: Ingestion Layer Controls
subsections.content:
- Content scanning: detect embedded instructions, PII, malicious URLs
- Document hashing: SHA-256 hash each document at ingestion for integrity tracking
- Source verification: allowlist trusted document sources; flag or reject unknown sources
- Metadata enforcement: require author, classification, and date on all documents
- Human review queue: flag documents with anomalous instruction-like patterns for review

subsections.title: Retrieval Layer Controls
subsections.content:
- User-scoped queries: attach user permission filters to every vector database query
- Document ACL: store permission metadata alongside embeddings; filter before returning results
- Query logging: log all queries and retrieved document IDs for audit
- Retrieval anomaly detection: alert on queries retrieving unusually sensitive documents or high volumes

subsections.title: Output Layer Controls
subsections.content:
- Source citation: include retrieved document IDs/titles in every response
- PII detection: scan responses for sensitive data patterns before delivery
- Content policy: apply output content filters
- Exfiltration monitoring: alert on responses that contain large volumes of knowledge base content
- Response logging: store all responses with their source documents for audit trail

content_blocks.title: Teach Me Like I'm 10: RAG Defense
content_blocks.content: Going back to the library analogy — securing the smart assistant who reads from a filing cabinet.

subsections.title: The defenses
subsections.content:
Ingestion scanning: before any new file goes in the cabinet, a security guard reads it for hidden instructions or false information.

Access control at retrieval: the assistant checks your access badge before pulling any file from the cabinet — not after already reading it.

Provenance tracking: every answer includes which files were used: 'Based on Q4 Budget Policy (HR-only document)' — so you'd know if restricted files were accessed.

Output monitoring: a supervisor reviews every answer for signs that the assistant was manipulated or is revealing things they shouldn't.

content_blocks.title: Implementing Retrieval-Time Access Control
content_blocks.description: Add user permission filtering to a vector database query
content_blocks.code:
from typing import List

# Example using LlamaIndex-style metadata filtering

def secure_retrieve(query: str, user: User, vector_store) -> List[Document]:
    # Build permission filter from user's roles/groups
    permitted_classifications = get_user_permitted_classifications(user)
    
    # Apply filter AT retrieval time — not after
    metadata_filter = {
        'classification': {'$in': permitted_classifications},
        # Additional filters: department, project, etc.
    }
    
    # Query with filter embedded — restricted docs never fetched
    results = vector_store.similarity_search(
        query=query,
        k=5,
        filter=metadata_filter  # <-- This is the key control
    )
    
    # Audit log: query, user, retrieved doc IDs
    audit_log(user.id, query, [doc.metadata['id'] for doc in results])
    
    return results

# WRONG approach — access control after retrieval:
def insecure_retrieve(query, user, vector_store):
    all_results = vector_store.similarity_search(query, k=5)
    # LLM has already seen restricted content in context!
    return [r for r in all_results if user_can_access(user, r)]
content_blocks.instructions:
1. Identify user permission attributes (roles, groups, clearance levels)
2. Store permission metadata alongside document embeddings at ingestion
3. Build permission filter objects for each user/query combination
4. Pass filters to the vector store query — not as a post-processing step
5. Log all retrievals with user ID and document IDs for audit
content_blocks.expected_outcome: Restricted documents are never included in LLM context for unauthorized users. The key insight: filtering must happen before documents reach the LLM, not after.

content_blocks.title: Microsoft Copilot for Microsoft 365 Security Architecture
content_blocks.scenario: Microsoft's Copilot for M365 applies permissions from SharePoint and OneDrive at retrieval time. The system only retrieves documents the authenticated user already has permission to read. This was a deliberate architectural decision — early testing showed that without retrieval-time access control, users could receive information from documents they weren't supposed to access via semantic queries. Microsoft's architecture became the reference implementation for enterprise RAG access control.
key_lessons: Retrieval-time access control is the industry-standard approach for enterprise RAG
Permission inheritance from existing document systems (SharePoint, Jira) is the practical implementation path
Even Microsoft needed explicit design focus to get this right
The existing permission model of your document system should be the source of truth for RAG ACLs

content_blocks.title: Secure RAG Architecture: SIPA
content_blocks.explanation: S=Scan ingestion (content integrity, instruction detection, PII, malicious URLs before any document enters KB), I=Identity-filtered retrieval (user permissions applied at query time, never post-retrieval), P=Provenance tracking (every response cites its source documents for auditability), A=Anomaly monitoring (alert on unusual retrieval patterns, high-volume responses, or restricted document access).

content_blocks.title: You Now Have the Full RAG Security Picture
content_blocks.content: Over the last three lessons, you've learned RAG architecture, attack techniques, and now defenses. You understand the full threat model. You can threat model a RAG system, find its vulnerabilities, and design controls for each one. This end-to-end knowledge is rare — most practitioners know one piece. You know all three. Apply it.
